submissions.findingTextShort: Chronic glycyrrhizic-acid exposure increased blood pressure and lowered potassium-related endocrine markers.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies involving 337 participants consuming products with at least 100 mg per day glycyrrhizic acid found increases in systolic and diastolic blood pressure together with lower plasma potassium, renin activity, and aldosterone, with blood-pressure effects related to glycyrrhizic-acid exposure.
submissions.populationContext: Participants across 18 human studies with glycyrrhizic-acid exposure
submissions.usageContext: Licorice/glycyrrhizic-acid-containing products at chronic exposures of at least about 100 mg/day glycyrrhizic acid
submissions.safetyContext: Supports clinically relevant blood-pressure and potassium-risk framing for glycyrrhizin-containing licorice.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Exposure composition and susceptibility vary; this should not be inherited unchanged by verified deglycyrrhizinated products.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 26-trial synthesis found a pooled diastolic blood-pressure increase with licorice exposure.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial-sequential analysis of 26 clinical trials involving 985 participants found a pooled increase in diastolic blood pressure with licorice exposure; small body-weight or BMI signals in the same literature should not be reframed as weight-loss benefit when cardiovascular and electrolyte safety is the higher-priority interpretation.
submissions.safetyContext: Supports blood-pressure caution and prevents marginal anthropometric signals from dominating general consumer guidance.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Preparation and glycyrrhizin content varied across trials, limiting one universal exposure threshold.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2024 meta-analysis found blood-pressure increases for glycyrrhizic-acid-dominant interventions but not licorice-flavonoid-dominant interventions.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of eight randomized trials involving 541 participants found significantly higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure with glycyrrhizic-acid-dominant interventions, while licorice-flavonoid-dominant interventions did not show statistically significant blood-pressure changes in the reported pooled analysis; licorice safety therefore depends materially on preparation composition.
submissions.populationContext: Participants across eight randomized trials with composition-distinct licorice interventions
submissions.uncertaintyNote: This preparation contrast does not establish that all flavonoid-dominant or DGL products are universally safe; each composition still needs its own evidence.
